title: Matt Sams
text:
Hey, I’m Matt. I moonlight as a performance analyst in America’s favorite pastime. In previous lives, I’ve worked in football, spent a little time as a professor, and spent a really long time as an applied sport scientist/S&C coach. I’ve had the chance to work with athletes in a range of sports, including soccer, basketball, volleyball, bobsled and skeleton, and XC skiing.
My main focus is on maximizing player performance while managing fatigue and injury risk. To that end, I’ve spent a lot of time developing and implementing athlete monitoring systems, building data visualizations and reports for stakeholders at all organizational levels, and performing in-depth post-mortem analyses to drive future decisions.

title: Across the Years 2024-2025 6-Day Race Recap
text: I’m not one to half-ass things, and that couldn’t be truer than my decision to run ATY’s 6-day race as my first-ever ultra-distance event–a decision that left other runners in varying degrees of shock when I would mention it in conversation. I tried to make it clear to these folks that I wasn’t coming in to the event blind. In fact, I spent nearly the entirety of 2024 training specifically for ATY and am hoping to do some post-mortem blogs about my training once I get a little separation from everything. But before I get ahead of myself (and while memories are still fresh), let’s talk about my experience at the event.

title: Across the Years 2024-2025 6-Day Race Recap
text:
Matt’s Learnings

What sets competitors apart from us mere mortals is resilience and consistency. In the case of Marc Sanderson (the winner, 457.8 mi [736.6 km]), that’s being able to run-walk at a near-constant pace for 16 hours a day. For Yolanda Holder (2nd place female, 401.5 mi [646 km]), that’s walking 285 laps at nearly the same pace. Oh yeah, and she probably slept fewer than 15 hours across the 6 days. I’ll never be a Yolanda (I need my beauty sleep), so I have to be a Marc. That means lots of run-walk practice in all sorts of conditions–fresh, fatigued, hot, cold, day, night–and not throwing the baby out with the bath water at the first sign of things not going perfectly.
At the same time, I should spend more time talking to other participants. We’re all there to push ourselves, but we’re there to do it together.
Speaking of, I need to spend more time going to group runs instead of always running in my neighborhood.
I need to be proactive about finding ultra distance-compatible shoes. I was in Saucony Triumph 20s (now discontinued), which have always been great for shorter sessions, but they did not get along with my feet after the first day. The sole created hotspots in all the wrong places, I couldn’t get the laces tightened in a way that accommodated swelling while keeping my heel locked in, and the tongues dug into my ankles constantly. I’ve always been a single-shoe runner for my training runs, but I need to explore my options as the paces and distances change.
I desperately need to strength train more consistently. The knee, while definitely owing some pain to the shoe fiasco, was absolutely a downstream effect of weak glutes forcing other muscle groups to compensate. I already did strength training session one today and am planning to keep a cadence of 2 sessions per week.
1/2 cup of maltodextrin + 1/4 cup table sugar + a pinch of salt beats any of your fancy gels…as long as I alternate that with some Gnarly Hydrate. Seriously, that’s the only electrolyte drink I’ve ever had where I wasn’t dying 30 minutes after drinking it.
